claims.text: High-temperature in-situ X-ray diffraction can capture both oxidation behavior and phase stability.
HT-XRD directly reveals the evolution of crystalline phases under oxidative conditions.
The proposed initial material is a ceramic or metal oxide with a well-defined room-temperature phase composition.
The sample will be exposed to a controlled high-temperature oxidative environment during in-situ XRD measurements.
The proposed temperature range is from ambient temperature to approximately 800–1200°C.
Controlled oxygen partial pressure can be used to simulate industrial or service environments.
Formation, transformation, or disappearance of crystalline phases produces changes in the XRD diffraction pattern.
High-temperature oxidation causes chemical reactions that form new oxide phases.
HT-XRD can detect oxidation-related phase transitions in real time through diffraction-peak shifts.
Diffraction-pattern changes can be correlated with oxidation kinetics.
The onset of oxidation will appear as new diffraction peaks or shifts in existing peaks.
New or shifted diffraction peaks will correspond to oxide formation or oxidation-linked phase transformations.
Insufficient XRD resolution may prevent detection of subtle phase transitions or minor secondary phases.
The performance and results of HT-XRD can vary among material systems.
Sample heterogeneity and oxygen diffusion rates can affect phase-change temperatures, kinetics, and the correlation between XRD signals and oxidation behavior.
Time-resolved weight gain measured by TGA can serve as an independent oxidation marker for comparison with XRD changes.
